# Overview

This document serves as the main reproducible report and computational workflow for Hemingway, C. et al. (202X). *Accounting for the unaccounted: a new framework for incorporating farm social diversity in micro-regional water budgets*. [Journal Name]. [DOI Link].

The **The Blue Water Potential Toolkit** provides a generalized R framework for simulating Blue Water Potential (Gross Groundwater Recharge minus Irrigation Requirement) at plot, farm, and village/micro-regional scale. By coupling climate, soil and crop information with socio-agricultural data, this toolkit computes and displays water fluxes, revealing how different types of farms can be either net consumers or net producers of blue water in a given climate. 

While this specific implementation is configured to reproduce the results and figures for the manuscript, the underlying R code is highly modular. It is designed to be easily adaptable for any case study globally, provided you have local meteorological and cropping system data. 

> 💡 **Using this Toolkit:** See the repository `README.md` for full instructions on how to adapt this framework using your own processed site data and how to cite this toolkit.

---

### 🗂️ Data Architecture & Workflow

This script acts as the primary **Analytical Engine**. It bridges the user's static inputs with the dynamically generated phenology curves:
1. It reads the static weather, soil, and demographic data directly from `data/input/`.
2. It pairs them with the derived phenology ($K_c$) curves from `data/processed/` (which were generated by `01_Prepare_Model_Input.qmd`).
3. It executes the multi-decadal water budget simulations and automatically routes the results and publication-ready visualizations to the `output/` and `figures/` directories.

### 📂 Directory Structure for this Script

This script assumes you have already placed your CSVs in `data/input/` and run `01_Prepare_Model_Input.qmd`. To run this script and generate the report, open the `.Rproj` and click "Render".

```text
project_root/
├── data/
│   ├── input/                       <- Required: Static parameters (Climate, Soil, Demographics)
│   └── processed/                   <- Required: Dynamic curves from the 01_Input script
│       ├── 01_crop.systems.l.kc.csv
│       └── supplementary/01_crop_kc_by_doy_all_crops.csv
├── code/
│   ├── functions/                   <- Required: Core toolkit dependencies
│   │   ├── 02_get_Peff.R      
│   │   ├── 03_get_budget.R
│   │   ├── 04_get_figures.R
│   │   └── 05_case_study_formatters.R
│   ├── 01_Format_Input_Data.qmd     <- Run 1st: Generates processed Kc curves
│   └── 02_Blue-Water.qmd            <- (This file)
├── output/                          <- Generated: Final budget CSV summaries 
├── figures/                         <- Generated: Root folder for all visualizations
│   ├── manuscript/                  <- Generated: High-res print-ready PDFs
│   └── presentation/                <- Generated: Screen-ready PNGs and web layouts
├── Blue-Water.Rproj                 <- Required: RStudio Project file to render this script
└── 02_Blue-Water.html               <- Generated: HTML Report created by rendering this script
```

## User Configuration

If you are running this script for your own data but you don't have data at all scales, you can limit the scale of the analyses here.

The main Water Budget function calculations can be turned ON/OFF here. 

```{r, user-config}

# ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
# 2. If applying for your study site, is production or production as well as agrarian system scale data missing? ----
# ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

# By default, the script runs the full suite at village/micro-region (requires files processed/01 to 09 mentioned above in the 📂 Directory Structure for this Script).

# Set this if you have limited data!
HAS_PRODUCTION_SYSTEM <- TRUE # Set to FALSE to Stop at Cropping Systems (requires ONLY processed/01 to 07 data files).
HAS_AGRARIAN_SYSTEM <- TRUE # Set to FALSE to Stop at Production Systems (requires ONLY processed/01 to 08 data files).

# The main Water Budget Calculator function can be turned ON/OFF here. 
CALCULATE_BUDGET <- FALSE # Toggle this to FALSE, for example, if you have already run the water budget calculations once (so budget outputs are saved), and are manipulating the output processing code.
```

# Water Budget Calculator

We first transform precipitation series into site-specific effective inputs ($P_{eff}$), governed by the SCS Curve Number ($CN$) depending on soil type to account for surface runoff, before initializing the core water budget calculator.

```{r set_param_budget}
p.list <- base::list(
  precip = precip,
  et0 = et0,
  et0.timestep = et0.timestep, # Weekly or daily
  soil.input = get_param("soil_input", FALSE), # For the case study in Hemingway et al (202X), we assume effective precipitation (Peff) = precipitation. So, calculated Peff is not being used. Set soil.input <- "Peff", if you want to get runoff.
  soil.param = soil.param,
  sm.init = get_param("sm_init"), # Initial soil water content
  crop.param = crop.param,
  # Kc value depending on seasons governing bare-soil evaporation. 
  kc_no_crop = KC_FALLOW_CONSTANTS # Given in section # Kc Curves for Crop Systems
)

# The Water Budget Calculator operates on individual rotations
crop.rotation.kc.ls <- base::split(crop.systems.l.kc, crop.systems.l.kc$rotation)

# Vectorized generation of effective precipitation models across targeted soil horizons
met.forcing.ls <- base::lapply(base::as.list(soil.param$soil), function(x) {
  get_peff_et0(p = p.list, soil_id = x)
})
base::names(met.forcing.ls) <- soil.param$soil
```

> **Parallel Processing**
> Simulating multi-decadal daily water fluxes across dozens of crop rotations is computationally expensive. The code block below detects the number of available physical cores on your machine and parallelizes the tasks, drastically reducing execution time.

When the calculator finishes running, all daily data outputs are saved as well as aggregated by year (and month) as well as summaries across years (and months) in a single Rdata file:<br>
"output/01_processed_water_budgets.Rdata"

```{r budget-calculator}
#| eval: !expr CALCULATE_BUDGET
# Multi-Core Setup
num_cores <- parallel::detectCores(logical = FALSE) 
cl <- parallel::makeCluster(num_cores, type = "PSOCK")

parallel::clusterExport(cl, varlist = c("p.list", "met.forcing.ls", "get_budget"), envir = environment())
invisible(parallel::clusterEvalQ(cl, {library(tidyverse); library(ggpubr); library(here)}))

# Process budget arrays iteratively
budget <- pbapply::pblapply(crop.rotation.kc.ls, get_budget, cl = cl, p = p.list, ts = met.forcing.ls)
parallel::stopCluster(cl)

names(budget) <- names(crop.rotation.kc.ls)
base::save(budget, file = here::here("output/01_processed_water_budgets.Rdata"))
```

```{r load-precalculated-budgets}
# Internal loading mechanism to bypass lengthy re-calculations during document knitting
# (Ensure the Calculator block has been run at least once locally)
base::load(file = here::here("output/01_processed_water_budgets.Rdata"))

```

# Output Processing & BWP Calculations

We transform the "output/01_processed_water_budgets.Rdata") file into CSVs of:<br>
1. Daily outputs: "output/02_export_detailed_daily_water_budgets.csv",<br>
2. Yearly outputs: "output/03_export_annual_water_budgets_long.csv", and<br>
3. For an average year (with SD across years):<br>
3.1. All water budget variables:<br>
"output/04_crop_system_water_budget_outputs_for_an_avg_year_with_sd.csv"<br>
3.2. Only Blue Water Potential:<br>
"output/05_crop_system_blue_water_potential_for_an_avg_year_with_sd.csv"

```{r compile-outputs}
# 1. Optimize Daily Processing
budget.daily.ls <- lapply(budget, function(x) {return(x$ts)})

# data.table::rbindlist is exponentially faster than dplyr::bind_rows for large lists
budget.daily <- data.table::rbindlist(budget.daily.ls, idcol = "rotation") %>% 
  dplyr::left_join(crop.systems, by = "rotation")

# readr::write_csv is massively faster than base write.csv
readr::write_csv(budget.daily, file = here::here("output/02_export_detailed_daily_water_budgets.csv"))

# 2. Optimize Annual Processing
budget.yr.ls <- lapply(budget, function(x) {return(x$sum.yr)})
budget.yr.l <- data.table::rbindlist(budget.yr.ls, idcol = "rotation") %>% 
    tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = c(-rotation, -year), names_to = "var", values_to = "value") %>%
    dplyr::left_join(crop.systems, by = "rotation")

readr::write_csv(budget.yr.l, file = here::here("output/03_export_annual_water_budgets_long.csv"))

# Save water budget outputs an average year (with median and 95% quantiles across years)
summary_yr_budgets <- process_annual_budget(budget, crop.systems)
summ.qs.cs <- summary_yr_budgets$summ_qs_cs

readr::write_csv(summ.qs.cs, file = here::here("output/04_crop_system_water_budget_outputs_for_an_avg_year_with_sd.csv"))

# Process the Blue Water Potential (BWP)
bwp <- summ.qs.cs %>% 
  base::subset(var == "balance") %>%
  dplyr::select(-var, -var.plot)
colnames(bwp)[-c(1,2)] <- paste0("BWP_", colnames(bwp)[-c(1,2)])

readr::write_csv(bwp, file = here::here("output/05_crop_system_blue_water_potential_for_an_avg_year_with_sd.csv"))
```

# Blue Water Potential at Production System Scale

Here we show the aggregated Blue Water Potential of the different cropping systems within each production system (social category of farmer),  

> 🔍 **Understanding Net Consumers vs. Net Producers**
>
> * **Production Systems with $BWP < 0$:** are Net Consumers of groundwater in the current climate of the study site because their irrigation demand exceeds gross recharge over their area. On the long term they can sustain only if groundwater recharge is supplied by others inside or outside the watershed.
>
> * **Production Systems with ($BWP > 0$):** are Net Producers of groundwater in the current climate of the study site because either they are fully rainfed or because their area under irrigation is small compared to the rainfed area. On the long term they contribute to the Blue Water Commons of the area that help sustains the Net Consumers.
> 
> 

```{r Run_Aggregation}
#| eval: !expr HAS_PRODUCTION_SYSTEM
ps_results <- get_production_system_budgets(budget.yr.l, ps_by_cs_area, farms_count_df)

ps_budget_summary  <- ps_results$ps_budget_summary
ps_volumetric_summary <- ps_results$ps_volumetric_summary
ps_bwp_volumetric <- ps_results$ps_bwp_volumetric

utils::write.csv(ps_bwp_volumetric, file = here::here("output/06_production_system_bwp_contributions.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r ann-social, eval=HAS_PRODUCTION_SYSTEM, fig.width=10, fig.height=5.65, out.width="100%", fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = 'Figure 6. Comparative annual Blue Water Potential ($BWP$) across Production Systems, or farm types, (1950s vs. 2022). BWP contributions (+ve or -ve) from Irrigated/Rainfed cropped area, or grazed area within each farm type are mapped by colors. Net BWP contribution of each farm type is identified by a cross.'}
fig.6_social <- plot_production_system_bwp(ps_bwp_volumetric)
print(fig.6_social)

# Save PDF for Manuscript
ggplot2::ggsave(here::here("figures/manuscript/Fig.6_Socio_Economic_Group_BWP.pdf"), fig.6_social, width = 10, height = 5.65, device = grDevices::cairo_pdf)

# Save PNG for Presentation
ggplot2::ggsave(here::here("figures/presentation/Fig.6_Socio_Economic_Group_BWP.png"), fig.6_social, width = 10, height = 5.65, dpi = 300, bg = "white", device = ragg::agg_png)
```

# Blue Water Potential at Agrarian System Scale

## Contribution of Production Systems to Annual Blue Water Potential at Village Scale

Finally, we aggregate the Blue Water Potential of all the production systems, or Social Categories of Farmers, to understand how they contribute to the Blue Water Potential of the agrarian system. In the case study of Hemingway et al. 202X, this is done at the scale of the archetype village, at two historical periods: 1950s and 2022. In the 1950s, all the social category had a positive Blue Water Potential (and were thus Net Producers), while in 2022 the social categories are divided in Net Consumers and Net Producers.

This figure highlights the role of often ignored social category such as Pastoralists who in 2022 are main Net Contributers of Blue Water in the archetype village.

## Classical Representation of Water Balance

Here we illustrate how water balance is commonly represented as aggregated Inflows minus Outflows by land-use. In contrast to the new framework (as illustrated in the last figure), here all land uses are represented as net water consumers. This representation ignores the complementarity between land-uses for the Blue Water Balance at the village/micro-regional scale and can lead to maladaptive management decisions (e.g., getting rid of pastoral systems, or replacement of rainfed crops by irrigated crops).


```{r village-budget, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.align='center', fig.cap="Figure 8. Average annual water balance of the archetype village.", message = FALSE}
#| eval: !expr HAS_AGRARIAN_SYSTEM
#| 
classical_budget_fig_data <- format_agrarian_sankey_data(ps_volumetric_summary)

# --- DEFINE YOUR PREFERRED MARGINS HERE ---
# Margins for the interactive HTML document
html_margin_left  <- 10
html_margin_right <- 30

# Margins specifically for the PNG/PDF printout
# (Adjust these if the camera export needs different spacing)
export_margin_left  <- 50
export_margin_right <- 50
# ------------------------------------------

# 1. Build the HTML version
sankey_1950_html <- get_d3_sankey(classical_budget_fig_data, "1950", font_size = 14, margin_left = html_margin_left, margin_right = html_margin_right)
sankey_2022_html  <- get_d3_sankey(classical_budget_fig_data, "2022", font_size = 14, margin_left = html_margin_left, margin_right = html_margin_right)

combined_panels_html <- htmltools::tagList(
  htmltools::tags$div(
    style = "display: flex; flex-direction: row; justify-content: space-between; width: 100%;",
    htmltools::tags$div(
      style = "width: 48%;",
      htmltools::tags$h3("A. 1950s Archetype Village", style = "text-align: center; font-family: sans-serif; font-size: 16px;"),
      sankey_1950_html
    ),
    htmltools::tags$div(
      style = "width: 48%;",
      htmltools::tags$h3("B. 2022 Archetype Village", style = "text-align: center; font-family: sans-serif; font-size: 16px;"),
      sankey_2022_html
    )
  )
)

  # 2. Build a completely separate Export version with its own margins
  sankey_1950_export <- get_d3_sankey(classical_budget_fig_data, "1950", font_size = 14, margin_left = export_margin_left, margin_right = export_margin_right)
  sankey_2022_export  <- get_d3_sankey(classical_budget_fig_data, "2022", font_size = 14, margin_left = export_margin_left, margin_right = export_margin_right)
  
  combined_panels_export <- htmltools::tagList(
    htmltools::tags$div(
      style = "display: flex; flex-direction: row; justify-content: space-between; width: 100%;",
      htmltools::tags$div(
        style = "width: 48%;",
        htmltools::tags$h3("A. 1950s Archetype Village", style = "text-align: center; font-family: sans-serif; font-size: 16px;"),
        sankey_1950_export
      ),
      htmltools::tags$div(
        style = "width: 48%;",
        htmltools::tags$h3("B. 2022 Archetype Village", style = "text-align: center; font-family: sans-serif; font-size: 16px;"),
        sankey_2022_export
      )
    )
  )
  
  html_path <- here::here("temp_combined_sankey.html")
  png_path  <- here::here("figures/presentation/Fig.8_Village_Sankey.png")
  pdf_path  <- here::here("figures/manuscript/Fig.8_Village_Sankey.pdf")
  
  # Save the EXPORT version for the camera
  htmltools::save_html(combined_panels_export, html_path)
  
try({
    # Changed zoom from 2 to 4 to generate a 300+ DPI publication-quality image
    webshot2::webshot(url = html_path, file = png_path, vwidth = 1250, vheight = 600, zoom = 4, delay = 5)
    
    # Save perfectly framed, ultra-high-res PNG into PDF format
    if (file.exists(png_path)) {
      img <- png::readPNG(png_path)
      grDevices::pdf(pdf_path, width = 14, height = 6)
      graphics::par(mar = c(0,0,0,0)) 
      graphics::plot.new()
      graphics::rasterImage(img, 0, 0, 1, 1)
      invisible(grDevices::dev.off())
    }
  }, silent = TRUE)
  base::unlink(html_path)

# 3. Print the HTML version to your actual knitted document
combined_panels_html
```


## Impact of Social Category Demographics on Blue Water Potential of the Village

This figure shows how some social category (Production System) disproportionately affect the Blue Water Potential of the village/micro-region.

For the case study in Hemingway et al. 202X, a large number of rainfed farmers and a few pastoralists have a large positive impact, while a few numbers of Small- and Large-scale fruit growers are the main Blue Water Consumers.


```{r disparity-plot, fig.width=11, fig.height=5.5, out.width="100%", fig.align = 'center', fig.cap = 'Figure 9. Number of farmers in each Production System (left panel) and their aggregated Blue Water Potential (BWP) (right panel; in thousand m³).'}
